title: Anthropic sets IPO price range at 70 to 78 dollars, targets Nasdaq debut November 19
subtitle: The amended S-1 offers 825 million shares under the ticker ANT at a range that implies up to a 1.4 trillion dollar fully diluted valuation. AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia, and TSMC have agreed to a 26 billion dollar concurrent private placement of Class N stock.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Anthropic launched its IPO roadshow this week and filed an amended prospectus setting a price range of 70 to 78 dollars per share on 825 million shares, with pricing expected around November 18 and a Nasdaq debut targeted for November 19 under the ticker ANT. At the high end of the range the offering values Anthropic at roughly 1.4 trillion dollars on a fully diluted basis. Separately, seven strategic partners — AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia, and TSMC — have agreed to purchase 26 billion dollars of Class N common stock in a concurrent private placement; that stock sits outside the public float and carries its own transfer restrictions. Early demand in the book is reported to cover the range on an allocable basis, though that figure comes from anonymous sources rather than the filing.

The structure is the story. A 26 billion dollar private placement from the companies that sell Anthropic its chips, memory, foundry capacity, and cloud compute binds the AI supply chain to Anthropic's equity in a way the public tape alone would not. It is also a message to the market: the people who know the compute curve best are willing to take the risk at this valuation. The S-1 mentions compute roughly 49 times, highlights a long-term target operating margin of about 35 percent, and lays out the existential-risk language that regulators and plaintiffs' lawyers have already pulled quotes from — including the nonprofit lawsuit filed in San Francisco on November 12. The dual message of ambition and risk disclosure is deliberate; it is how Anthropic has consistently framed itself, and the IPO is the first time that framing is being priced.

The timing is sharp. Nvidia has lost its CEO this week and tens of billions in market value; a coalition of nonprofits has asked a California court to enjoin frontier model development; and the broader AI tape has traded heavily for a month. Anthropic is pushing into that environment with a book-covered offering backed by the dominant strategic buyers in the industry, which is both the strongest signal of confidence imaginable and a reminder that this market is not an ordinary tech IPO. If ANT prices at the top and trades up, the implied narrative is that compute-backed AI labs have durable scarcity value even at trillion-dollar marks. If it prices at the low end or breaks, the industry-wide repricing will be loud.

A takeaway for learners: read the risk factors section of an AI lab's S-1 the way you would read a model card. The material on compute dependence, safety commitments, and legal exposure is where you will find the honest view of the business. If you want to follow AI as an industry — as an engineer, a researcher, or a future founder — spend an hour with Anthropic's amended S-1 before November 19. It is one of the clearest primary-source descriptions of how a frontier lab describes itself to the people who are about to own it.
